A_target.statement:
Let $\struct {X, d}$ be a [[Definition:Complete Metric Space|complete metric space]].
Let $T: X \to X$ satisfy:
:$\forall x, y \in X: \map d {T x, T y} \le k \, \map d {x, y}$
for some $k \in \hointr 0 1$.
Then $T$ has a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] [[Definition:Fixed Point|fixed point]], which is the [[Definition:Limit of Sequence|limit]] of $\sequence {T^n x_0}$ for every $x_0 \in X$.

B_source.statement:
Let $f: \closedint a b \to \closedint a b$ satisfy:
:$\forall x, y \in \closedint a b: \size {\map f x - \map f y} \le k \size {x - y}$
for some $k < 1$.
Then $f$ has a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] [[Definition:Fixed Point|fixed point]].

derived.convergence of the iterates: the iterates form a Cauchy sequence and converge by completeness
derived.uniqueness on the interval: uniqueness in the metric space, by the same contraction estimate

object_map.reformulation: Abstract from the real line to a complete metric space, keeping only the triangle inequality and completeness.

validity_conditions: The interval case is exactly the special case of the real line with the usual metric, so the generalization is faithful.
The proof uses only the triangle inequality and completeness, never the order or the local compactness of the interval, so it transfers without modification.
Completeness cannot be dropped: a contraction on a non-complete space may have Cauchy iterates with no limit in the space.
proof_plan: Replace $\closedint a b$ by the [[Definition:Complete Metric Space|complete metric space]] $\struct {X, d}$, and $\size {x - y}$ by $\map d {x, y}$.

Let $x_0 \in X$ and $x_{n + 1} = T x_n$.
By [[Principle of Mathematical Induction|induction]]:
